doc.title: Kidd Jordan interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 24, 2006

title: Playing the sound of the song, not the changes
summary: Jordan argues he plays the sound of a tune rather than spelling chords; Bird versus Sonny Stitt and the piano influence on saxophone.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: what I alluded to at the beginning. You’ve got to know how you work, how you are inside and how you work in opposed to how the other people do some things. And like sometimes a guy says, “man you’re not playing the changes.” I say, “I might not be playing the changes but I’m playing the sound of the song.

Well yeah, the song has a — the tune has a sound. If you play the sound of the tune I mean the changes are just bringing it through the tune. And if they hook up you do that. So if you’ve got to spell out every chord then you’re dealing with a formula. And Bird dealt with a formula but Bird didn’t do it like that. And some of them who came after him felt the difference between Bird and Sonny Stitt. Sonny sounded like Sonny Stitt. But Sonny Stitt played one way and Bird played another. I mean what Sonny was dealing with, a lot of people say, but Bird has some extra thing. And then another thing that I peeped a long time ago, that a lot of people play the saxophone, a lot of that music was concocted off of pianos. Bud Powell, you know how Bud Powell and them play?
